builder_plan.scenario: A support or data assistant repeats work across related customer requests.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's memory change in a replay of past tasks, with separate memory per customer.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current memory pipeline plus a no-memory control using the same agent.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, stale memories, retrieval misses, response latency, and all memory maintenance costs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
summary: The technique replaces blind history cleaning (compaction, repair, or handoff that rewrites past mistakes as resolved) with edits whose phrasing is checked against the actual world state, such as truthful annotations that preserve the error rather than completed-action claims. It costs added complexity in the compaction pipeline, since the editor must query or track world state before rewriting history, and it offers no latency or memory savings. It can fail when the system cannot verify world state at edit time, because a clean-looking history describing an error the world still holds leaves the continuing agent worse off than an unedited history.
rationale: Any production agent using context compaction or history rewriting faces exactly this failure mode, and the paper shows a cheap mitigation (truthful annotation instead of falsified completion) but only on two benchmarks, so the reader should validate the effect on their own workload before adopting it as policy.

claims.statement: The technique replaces blind history cleaning (compaction, repair, or handoff that rewrites past mistakes as resolved) with edits whose phrasing is checked against the actual world state, such as truthful annotations that preserve the error rather than completed-action claims. It costs added complexity in the compaction pipeline, since the editor must query or track world state before rewriting history, and it offers no latency or memory savings. It can fail when the system cannot verify world state at edit time, because a clean-looking history describing an error the world still holds leaves the continuing agent worse off than an unedited history.

On AgentCE-Bench, a truthful note beside a preserved error raises receiver recovery from 51% to 66%, while writing the correction as a completed action lowers it from 50% to 44%; on AppWorld, a success receipt for an absent effect drops whole-task success from 45% to 28%, versus a rise from 38% to 49% when the effect is present (27-point pooled difference).
